transcript: Yeah, well, good question. Is politics on Capitol Hill ever normal, especially these days? You know, we came out of a tumultuous election year into a tumultuous start to the new cycle with the new president, a new Democrat-controlled Congress. I do think there was hope held out that there would be unity and bipartisanship as President Biden promised on the campaign trail that did not materialize. And so I think we're as partisan and divided as we've ever been, quite frankly, and that doesn't mean that I'm not working to cultivate the relationships with the likes of Henry Cuellar and other Democrats. I'm a co-chair of three caucuses that are bipartisan, and my relationships are as good as they've ever been, and we just have to not be too distracted by the macro politics, and focus on the needs for the country, like the drought that we're experiencing in agriculture, like preparing for the Farm Bill, and lots to promote and defend, and sort of till the ground in preparation of the next farm bill, continuing to work in a bipartisan way to keep the pressure on China to make the structural reforms for fair trade practices. That's a huge market obviously for sorghum growers. So I don't let the macro politics distract me from doing the job that I'm supposed to do and that I feel like I've been doing for four years, which is work with whoever I can work with, where we have common ground for the good of West Texas in our country. Certainly a big a divide between what President Biden wants to do with the Green New Deal and some of the environmental extreme policies that I think would be detrimental to ag and energy in rural America. But again, every day is a new day. I try to look for those slivers, sometimes small slivers of common ground so we can do some good for the country in the midst of all this, you know, political hyper-partisanship.
